Resignation has two distinct meanings. Both share a hidden thread — the idea of giving something up or letting go — but they apply to very different situations. You need to know both.
Meaning 1: Voluntarily leaving a job or position

When a person chooses to leave their job, quit a role, or give up a position they hold, that act is called a resignation.

The critical word is voluntarily. A resignation is always the person's own decision. If someone is fired or removed by others, that is not a resignation. Resignation = you leaving on your own terms.

It applies broadly — leaving a job at a company, a politician stepping down from office, a member quitting a committee, an official withdrawing from a government role.

A resignation is usually formal. It's often put in writing as a resignation letter (also called a "letter of resignation") — a document that officially announces the person is leaving.

Examples:

  • "The CEO's resignation shocked the entire company." — The CEO chose to leave the role.
  • "She wrote her resignation and placed it on her manager's desk." — Here "resignation" refers to the letter itself.
  • "The minister's resignation came after weeks of scandal."

Common verb pairings:

  • Submit / hand in / tender a resignation → to formally give the letter to the relevant person
  • Accept a resignation → to officially acknowledge that someone is leaving
Meaning 2: Quiet, calm acceptance of something unpleasant

This is the more emotional, abstract meaning — and it's equally common, especially in literature and thoughtful writing.

When you face a difficult, painful, or unwanted situation that you cannot change, and you stop fighting it, stop resisting, and simply accept it — even if that acceptance feels sad or reluctant — that state of mind is called resignation.

Picture it this way: resignation is the feeling behind the thought, "I don't like this. I wish things were different. But they aren't, and there's nothing I can do — so I'll accept it and move on."

This is not cheerful, happy acceptance. It carries a quiet, slightly heavy, even defeated tone. You are not at peace with the situation; you have simply stopped fighting it. It is acceptance without joy.

Examples:

  • "He faced his illness with resignation, knowing the doctors could do nothing more." — He accepted his illness calmly, without bitterness, because fighting it was no longer possible.
  • "She signed the divorce papers with a sigh of resignation." — She accepted something painful that she could not undo.
  • "There was resignation in her voice as she said goodbye." — Her tone was that quiet, subdued sound of someone who has accepted something they cannot change.
  • "He shrugged with resignation and went back to work." — He accepted an annoying or unfair situation without making a fuss, because he knew it wouldn't change.

Common phrases with this meaning:

  • With resignation — in a tone or manner of quiet acceptance
  • A sense of resignation / a feeling of resignation — that emotional state of having stopped resisting
  • Resigned to something (the adjective form, related to this meaning) — having accepted something, e.g., "She was resigned to the fact that she wouldn't get the job."
How to tell which meaning is being used

Context makes it almost always obvious:

  • If the sentence involves a job, office, role, or position and someone is leaving it → Meaning 1
    • "His resignation from the board was unexpected."
  • If the sentence describes a feeling, attitude, reaction, or tone in the face of something difficult → Meaning 2
    • "She accepted the bad news with resignation."

Both meanings share a common core: letting go of something. In Meaning 1, you let go of a position or role. In Meaning 2, you let go of the struggle against something you cannot control. This is not a coincidence — it is what gives the word its depth. Whether you are leaving a job or accepting a painful reality, you are, in both cases, releasing your hold on something.

That is what resignation means — and now you know all of it.
